questions.corrige_markdown:
**Respiration** is the **chemical process by which food substances (mainly glucose) are broken down (oxidised) in the living cells to release energy** (stored as ATP) for life processes such as movement, growth, active transport and keeping warm. Respiration takes place in **all living cells, all the time**.

It is **aerobic** when oxygen is used (glucose is completely broken down, mostly in the mitochondria):

$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O + \text{energy}$

and **anaerobic** when no oxygen is used (partial breakdown, in the cytoplasm), with less energy released. Respiration must not be confused with **breathing** (ventilation), which only brings oxygen to the cells.

questions.enonce_markdown: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration. *(6 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Aerobic respiration | Anaerobic respiration |
|---|---|
| **Needs oxygen** | **Takes place without oxygen** |
| Glucose is **completely oxidised** | Glucose is **only partly broken down** |
| End products: **carbon dioxide and water** | End products: **lactic acid** (animals, muscles) or **ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide** (yeast, plants) |
| **Large amount of energy** released (about 38 ATP per glucose; 2880 kJ per mole) | **Small amount of energy** released (2 ATP per glucose; about 120 to 210 kJ per mole) |
| Occurs in the **cytoplasm and mitochondria** | Occurs in the **cytoplasm only** |
| Occurs in most organisms, all the time | Occurs in yeast, some bacteria, and in muscle cells during hard exercise (oxygen debt) |
| Does not produce harmful accumulation (CO$_2$ and water are removed) | Lactic acid builds up and causes muscle fatigue and cramp; alcohol is toxic in excess |

Similarity: both are enzyme-controlled reactions that break down glucose to release energy in living cells.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe an experiment to show that energy is released during respiration. *(9 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Experiment: heat is released by germinating seeds (respiring tissue).**

**Apparatus and materials:** two vacuum (thermos) flasks, two thermometers, cotton wool, germinating (soaked) bean or pea seeds, an equal mass of dead (boiled) seeds as a control, disinfectant (e.g. formalin) or dilute bleach to rinse the seeds, retort stand/clamp.

**Labelled diagram (to be drawn):** flask A containing living germinating seeds and flask B containing boiled seeds, each closed with a cotton wool plug through which a thermometer passes, its bulb in the middle of the seeds; labels: thermometer, cotton wool, germinating seeds, boiled (dead) seeds, vacuum flask.

**Procedure:**
1. Soak the seeds for a day so they begin to germinate. Boil another equal portion of seeds to kill them (the control).
2. Rinse both lots in a weak disinfectant to kill micro-organisms (bacteria and fungi), which would also respire and give out heat.
3. Fill flask A with the germinating seeds and flask B with the boiled seeds (the same mass in each). Insert a thermometer in each so that the bulb is among the seeds, and plug with cotton wool (which lets air in).
4. Record the initial temperature of each flask and keep both in the same place.
5. Read the temperature of each flask at intervals (for example every 12 hours) for 2 to 3 days.

**Results:** the temperature in flask A (living seeds) **rises** (for example from 25 to 30 degrees C), while that of flask B (dead seeds) stays at about room temperature.

**Conclusion:** the living seeds are respiring and **release energy as heat**; so energy is released during respiration. The control shows that the heat does not come from the flask or surroundings. The vacuum flask reduces loss of heat so that the rise can be detected.

**Precautions:** same mass and number of seeds, same starting temperature, disinfect the seeds, use vacuum flasks, plug with cotton wool, not completely sealed.
